classification.difficultyReason: Model doubled area, expand the square and use the quadratic formula to obtain an exact positive length.

questions.mappingNote: The context requires constructing the quadratic before applying the formula and selecting the physically valid root.
questions.methodNote: Use the formula from page 15 after expanding and collecting terms as in Example 2 on page 16; simplify the surd exactly.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model doubled area, expand the square and use the quadratic formula to obtain an exact positive length.

classification.difficultyReason: Model tripled area, simplify the resulting quadratic and select its positive exact root.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed skill is forming and solving a quadratic from a change in square area, with an exact surd answer.
questions.methodNote: Expand and collect terms following Example 2 on page 16, then substitute the coefficients into the quadratic formula from page 15.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model tripled area, simplify the resulting quadratic and select its positive exact root.

classification.difficultyReason: Model the two rectangle constraints, solve the resulting quadratic with a surd constant and interpret the complementary positive roots as dimensions.

questions.mappingNote: The most advanced directly assessed task is constructing a quadratic from two rectangle constraints and interpreting both exact roots as dimensions.
questions.methodNote: Form a standard quadratic by substitution and collecting terms, then apply the page 15 formula. Example 1(b) on page 15 supports surd coefficients; Example 2 on page 16 supports rearrangement before substitution.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine perimeter and area constraints, eliminate one length and simplify the quadratic formula with a surd coefficient.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate the geometric constraints into a quadratic and connect its negative discriminant to the impossibility of real rectangle dimensions.

questions.mappingNote: The rectangle context directly assesses quadratic modelling, with the discriminant establishing impossibility.
questions.methodNote: Form a quadratic in standard form and use the discriminant: a negative value means no real solutions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model area and perimeter, then use a negative discriminant to prove impossibility.

classification.difficultyReason: Show a parameter-dependent discriminant is strictly positive using the nonzero parameter condition.

questions.mappingNote: The parameters occur in the coefficients, and their stated conditions establish the sign of the discriminant.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate the discriminant and apply the positive-discriminant criterion for two distinct real solutions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Show a parameter-dependent discriminant is strictly positive using the nonzero parameter condition.

classification.difficultyReason: Form a parameter-dependent discriminant and choose completing the square to prove it stays strictly positive for every real parameter.

questions.mappingNote: The task requires proving a discriminant is positive for every real coefficient parameter.
questions.methodNote: Use completing the square, demonstrated in the formula derivation, to establish the discriminant's sign; apply the positive-discriminant criterion.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Complete the square in the discriminant to prove positivity for every real parameter.

classification.difficultyReason: Use coefficient signs and a nonnegative square to explain why the discriminant is positive.

questions.mappingNote: The coefficient signs determine the discriminant's sign without calculating the roots.
questions.methodNote: A positive discriminant gives two distinct real solutions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use coefficient signs and a nonnegative square to explain why the discriminant is positive.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate symbolic discriminants and use the nonzero parameter to justify their signs.

questions.mappingNote: Each part asks for the number of solutions from the sign of a symbolic discriminant; discriminant-nature-roots is the directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Use the discriminant b²−4ac and the three real-solution cases stated on page 16.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate symbolic discriminants and use the nonzero parameter to justify their signs.

classification.difficultyReason: Derive a two-parameter condition for a repeated root and exhaust the positive-integer factor pairs.

questions.mappingNote: The task requires finding unknown coefficients from the repeated-root condition, followed by a positive-integer restriction.
questions.methodNote: The discriminant equals zero precisely when a quadratic has one real solution.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Derive a two-parameter condition for a repeated root and exhaust the positive-integer factor pairs.

classification.difficultyReason: Derive the repeated-root condition in two parameters and enumerate all positive-integer factor pairs.

questions.mappingNote: Finding the parameter pairs from the discriminant is the principal assessment; the positive-integer condition bounds the final enumeration.
questions.methodNote: Set b²−4ac to zero for one real solution, using a=2m, b=mn and c=2n.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Derive the repeated-root condition in two parameters and enumerate all positive-integer factor pairs.

classification.difficultyReason: Simplify the symbolic discriminant to a squared difference and distinguish its zero and positive cases using the stated parameter conditions.

questions.mappingNote: The task relates parameter equality to the number of roots through a symbolic discriminant.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate the discriminant and apply the zero and positive cases from the taught real-solution criterion.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Express the discriminant as a square and interpret the equal and unequal parameter cases.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires a positive discriminant, integer parameter values and exclusion of a non-quadratic case.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed task is finding integer coefficient parameters from the discriminant.
questions.methodNote: Use the discriminant b²−4ac; a positive discriminant gives two distinct real solutions when the leading coefficient is nonzero.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires a positive discriminant, integer parameter values and exclusion of a non-quadratic case.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires denominator restrictions and proving that a resulting quadratic has no real roots.

questions.mappingNote: The proof depends on the nature of roots rather than merely simplifying the fractions.
questions.methodNote: Rearrange into quadratic form and use a negative discriminant to establish that no real solutions exist.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires denominator restrictions and proving that a resulting quadratic has no real roots.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise the repeated reciprocal sum as one variable, solve the outer quadratic and then solve both resulting inner quadratics while retaining all valid roots.

questions.mappingNote: The repeated expression x+1/x is the substitution that reduces the equation to quadratic form.
questions.methodNote: Reduce to quadratic equations and apply the quadratic formula, retaining exact surd answers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires substitution, two resulting quadratic equations and rejection of the branch with no real roots.

classification.difficultyReason: Treat the visibly repeated expression as a single variable, solve its quadratic and reverse the substitution with both square-root signs.

questions.mappingNote: Substitution u=x²+2 is the most advanced directly assessed step.
questions.methodNote: Apply the quadratic formula to the repeated expression, then solve the resulting square equations exactly.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires substitution for a repeated quadratic expression and recovery of both signs of x.

classification.difficultyReason: Discover that the conjugate bases are reciprocals, reduce to a quadratic and recognise the resulting surds as powers of a common base to recover x.

questions.mappingNote: The most advanced assessed step is reducing an exponential equation to a quadratic.
questions.methodNote: Identify coefficients, substitute into the quadratic formula and simplify exact surds, as in Examples 1–2. Reciprocal-base substitution is required by this enrichment question.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise reciprocal exponential bases, introduce a substitution and solve the resulting quadratic.

classification.difficultyReason: Uses Vieta’s formulas to evaluate symmetric expressions, including a sum of cubes.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly assess the supplied sum-and-product-of-roots skill; no individual roots need to be calculated.
questions.methodNote: Use Vieta’s formulas, then expansion and fraction combination to express each quantity through the sum and product of the roots. Page 19 Example 1 teaches the sum-of-squares identity; Example 2 teaches reciprocal addition.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Uses Vieta’s formulas to evaluate symmetric expressions, including a sum of cubes.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine fractions and rewrite squared-root expressions in terms of the known sum and product, extending the taught identities to shifted denominators.

questions.mappingNote: Each part evaluates an expression in the roots through their sum and product; the supplied catalogue skill is the direct match.
questions.methodNote: Use Vieta’s formulas and algebraic expansion or fraction combination. The reciprocal and sum-of-squares demonstrations on page 19 provide the methods extended to shifted expressions here.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Rewrites shifted products and rational expressions using Vieta’s formulas.

classification.difficultyReason: Derive sums and products of transformed roots using reciprocal and square identities, then reconstruct quadratics and clear coefficient denominators.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly assesses the sum and product of transformed quadratic roots.
questions.methodNote: Use Vieta’s formulas, derive transformed sums and products, then form x²−Sx+P and clear denominators.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Forms integer-coefficient quadratics from transformed root sums and products.

classification.difficultyReason: Uses shifted, scaled, cubed and rationally transformed roots to construct quadratics.

questions.mappingNote: Shifted and scaled roots use direct sum/product transformations; cubed and rational roots require identities before constructing the quadratic.
questions.methodNote: Apply Vieta’s formulas and algebraic identities to transformed root sums and products; form x²−Sx+P and clear denominators.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Uses shifted, scaled, cubed and rationally transformed roots to construct quadratics.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the root product to enumerate positive integer factor pairs and compare their sums to minimise the coefficient.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed constraint and minimisation depend directly on the coefficient/root relationships.
questions.methodNote: Vieta’s formulas identify the product as 40 and the sum as a; enumerate positive integer factor pairs.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Minimises the root sum by considering every positive integer factor pair of 40.

classification.difficultyReason: Enumerate unordered positive integer factor pairs, include the repeated-root pair and count the distinct coefficient sums they produce.

questions.mappingNote: Counting coefficient values requires the root sum/product relationships and includes the repeated-root pair.
questions.methodNote: Vieta’s formulas identify the product as 100 and the sum as a; enumerate factor pairs and count distinct sums.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Counts distinct root sums from all positive integer factor pairs, including equal roots.

classification.difficultyReason: Counts distinct products of positive integer root pairs with a fixed sum, including equal roots.

questions.mappingNote: The fixed root sum determines the positive integer pairs; their distinct products count the possible constant coefficients.
questions.methodNote: Vieta’s formulas give the sum and product of the roots directly from the coefficients.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Counts distinct products of positive integer root pairs with a fixed sum, including equal roots.

classification.difficultyReason: Finds a coefficient from the product of rationally transformed roots.

questions.mappingNote: The constant coefficient of the second monic quadratic equals the product of its transformed roots.
questions.methodNote: Use Vieta’s product formula, with the reciprocal-root manipulation illustrated by Example 2.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Finds a coefficient from the product of rationally transformed roots.

classification.difficultyReason: Relates the sums and products of roots of two quadratics under scaling.

questions.mappingNote: Root scaling determines the relationship between the linear coefficients and then between the constant coefficients.
questions.methodNote: Apply both Vieta formulas to compare coefficients through the roots.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Relates the sums and products of roots of two quadratics under scaling.

classification.difficultyReason: Converts a symmetric expression in the roots into a quadratic equation for an unknown coefficient.

questions.mappingNote: Factor the supplied symmetric expression, replace root sums and products by coefficients, and solve the resulting quadratic in k.
questions.methodNote: Use Vieta’s formulas and the identity for the sum of squared roots demonstrated in Example 1, with the necessary factor 2.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Converts a symmetric expression in the roots into a quadratic equation for an unknown coefficient.
